title: 'Some People May Believe It': Avi Loeb Slams the 'Clickbait' Claiming Aliens Are Arriving in 16 Days
excerpt: Avi Loeb rejects the 'aliens in 16 days' prediction as clickbait, explaining why it misrepresents his research and the evidence on 3I/ATLAS.
content:
Harvard astrophysicist Avi Loeb has rejected an online claim that he predicted aliens would reveal themselves within 16 days. In an interview with NewsNation's Jesse Weber Live on Thursday, 8 October 2026, he described the false attribution as an attempt to attract clicks.

His denial raises wider questions about how claims involving extraterrestrial life become detached from scientific evidence.

The disputed prediction circulated on social media accounts associated with pop culture and sport. The original author has not been independently established, and the available reporting identifies no statement in which Loeb announced such a countdown.

Avi Loeb Rejects the 16-Day Alien Prediction

Loeb said people were attributing remarks to him that he had never made. 'In this case, they wanted to get clickbait. They did get it,' he told NewsNation.

His concern extended beyond whether the posts attracted attention. 'Some people may believe it,' Loeb warned, pointing to the danger of readers accepting a statement merely because it carries a scientist's name.

The professor's criticism should not be confused with independent proof of who created the original claim or why. Those details remain unverified. What is clear is that he rejected the prediction outright.

Loeb has frequently explored whether unfamiliar astronomical observations could have unconventional explanations. Yet suggesting that an object deserves investigation is not equivalent to identifying extraterrestrial technology. It certainly does not establish when aliens might appear.

He has also accepted a documented $1,000 (£755.20) wager involving science historian Michael Shermer and a deadline of 31 December 2030. That bet concerns specified evidence of extraterrestrial visitation being confirmed by scientific organisations. It is not a promise that extraterrestrials will announce themselves within days.

How Avi Loeb's 3I/ATLAS Research Became Part of the Debate

Interest in Loeb's work intensified after the discovery of 3I/ATLAS, an object first reported on 1 July 2025. Loeb co-authored a paper examining whether it might have an artificial extraterrestrial origin. The paper presented that possibility as a hypothesis, not an observed discovery.

NASA identifies 3I/ATLAS as an interstellar comet. Its observations show an icy nucleus surrounded by a coma, the cloud of gas and dust associated with cometary activity. The agency says the object's observed characteristics are consistent with a comet, even though it arrived from beyond the solar system.

That difference is easily overlooked in social media discussions. Interstellar describes where an object came from. It does not establish that the object was designed, controlled or sent by an intelligent civilisation.

NASA has also said the comet posed no threat to Earth. At its nearest, 3I/ATLAS remained approximately 270 million kilometres from our planet. Neither its trajectory nor its classification provides evidence for the disputed 16-day prediction.

Astronomers Confront Misinformation Beyond the Avi Loeb Claim

The concern about misleading claims predates Loeb's television interview. On 23 February 2026, the International Astronomical Union announced a campaign to counter rumours and false information circulating about 3I/ATLAS.

The organisation said its Minor Planet Centre had received more than 4,000 observations of the object. It used that evidence to explain the comet's path and address claims that it might come close to Earth. The campaign offered validated information, public questions and answers, and educational material.

The union's announcement did not address the later allegation about Loeb's 16-day countdown. It does, however, illustrate a related problem. Spectacular claims can circulate faster than the observations needed to assess them.

Loeb's Galileo Project describes its aim as a systematic, scientifically validated search for possible extraterrestrial technological artefacts. Such a search leaves the question of alien technology open to investigation without treating every unusual observation as confirmation.

For the immediate claim, the evidence is narrower. Loeb says he did not make the prediction, and no authenticated statement from him supporting it has been established.

The larger scientific question remains open to research. But research into life beyond Earth is not a promise that aliens will reveal themselves on a specific day.
